beats.t: Far upstream from the bakery, where the current broke white against rocks, the black tiger crouched alone.
Twelve marks from black hands scarred its back. Wounds throbbed beneath the torn cloak. The tiger did not lick them. Licking them felt like admitting they hurt.
Instead, it felt inside its cloak. The paper-wrapped bread was still there. All the warmth had gone, leaving only its shape.
She said once it cooled, it was just bread.
It unfolded the note. Three crooked syllables spelled a name. The drumming child from the festival island. The child whose applause it had collected.
Are you still drumming? Even without applause?
The note did not answer. The tiger folded it again. Its fingertips were careful, different from the paw that closed the ledger.
It did not take out the bread. It checked another part of the cloak. The note with the drum boy's name. Bread beside it. Two things absent from the ledger now.
It opened the ledger. Yeoni's entry read No balance remaining. Yet beneath it, a faint line nobody had written was spreading.
[ Ledger · Eulhae Yeoni · Uncollected: 1 ]
Uncollected.
Money not received. Something still owed. The tiger scratched the line with a claw. It would not erase. It grew clearer instead.
What haven't I collected? I took everything. Even that child's tomorrows.
As it spoke, a touch returned. The child with nothing, pushing the ring with their forehead. The voice saying to say it hurt when it hurt.
What it had collected was fortune. Yet the ledger was recording that it had received something. Something it could not repay.
The ring on its right forepaw suddenly heated. Glowing red, the golden band tightened one notch, then another. Bone sounded under pressure.
Ghh.
A black fissure opened over the river. The gap into the other sky where it had been driven. From beyond, a voice flowed through the ring.
Tiger. That paw you wrapped around my vessel. Still attached, I see.
It is.
A pity. I should have taken it off.
The ring tightened again. The tiger did not scream. It drove its claws into the rock and held on. The rock cracked.
Why did you come to me? Do you remember?
To stop that child before they became a monster.
Yes. One day, that child will betray everyone. As they betrayed you. Who gave you the chance to prevent it?
You did.
Have you forgotten that kindness?
I haven't. Not for a day.
Yet today, you saved that child.
The tiger could not answer. Only the river sounded. It truly had no words. It did not know why it had done it.
Instead of an answer, a scene rose. Not one it had chosen. Whenever the ring tightened, this scene always spilled out.
A rainy bus stop. A wet bench. A hand tilting an umbrella halfway toward it. Rain always hid the face.
And then the next scene. That same hand pushing it away. A sense that something black and round had glimmered behind the hand's owner's eyes.
That feeling always broke off there. Black Moon's voice filled the gap. That child betrays. That child betrays.
One question. How much was that bread?
What?
I smell something inside your cloak. A smell absent from the ledger.
Without realizing, the tiger wrapped a paw around the cloak. That movement answered. Laughter came from beyond the fissure.
They called it free? Nothing is free. You know that best. That bread's price will be charged one day. In your blood.
I'll pay for the bread. Leave that bakery alone.
Oh? An order?
A request.
The ring tightened fiercely one last time. The tiger pitched forward, face plunging into the river. Cold water entered its nose.
I'll grant your request. In return, do your job.
The child has gone to the human world. That cat regained his human shell, too. Though not his name.
Go as well. With a human face. This time, finish it there.
My human face was lost long ago...
I'll return it. A loan. You know the interest.
Black fur streamed away like rain. Paws became hands, claws became nails. The ring did not vanish. It became a fine gold cord wound into the flesh of her right wrist.
The fissure closed. A woman with wet hair knelt on the riverbank. She still held the ledger.
She remained there a long time. Then searched her cloak, now a black coat. Inside its pocket, a note and a roll.
She took out the bread, removed the paper. Cold. She bit into it.
Cold bread. Yet it was sweet. It smelled of butter. A flavor no ledger could record spread slowly across her tongue.
Her shoulders trembled once. She did not cry. Only rainwater ran down her face.
She ate half, wrapped the other half again, and put it away. No one asked why. Even if someone had, she could not have answered.
A rainy night. A fluorescent light flickered in an old apartment corridor. Two homes at its end. Before one stood an umbrella holder with a torn corner.
A black umbrella was propped before the vacant home next door. Water dripped from its tip onto the floor.
The door opened, then closed. Only the smell of rain remained in the corridor.
The vacant apartment was empty. Dust covered the floor. Without turning on the light, the woman stood by the window. Water fell from her wet coat.
Sounds came through the thin wall. Something dropping onto the floor. Then a sleepy voice.
Neo, that's my sock. Don't throw it out. It's only a little hole.
The woman pressed a palm to the wall. The golden cord at her right wrist shone coldly. A low voice on the other side stopped short. As though someone had sensed her.
You two are noisy even here.
She withdrew her hand. Without removing her wet coat, she sat on the floor and leaned against the wall. Until the sounds beyond it faded.
The ledger lay open on her knees. One uncollected line glowed faintly in the dark. She looked at it for a long time, then shut the book.
